title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 28
paragraphs: Many historians say that the French did not win the battle of Borodino because Napoleon had a cold, and that if he hadn't had a cold, the orders he gave before and during the battle would have been even more brilliant, and Russia would have been lost and the face of the world changed. To historians who believe that Russia was shaped by the will of one man—Peter the Great—and that France became an empire and French armies marched into Russia by the will of one man—Napoleon—saying that Russia was saved because Napoleon had a bad cold on the twenty-fourth of August may seem logical and convincing.

If it had depended on Napoleon's will whether to fight or not fight the battle of Borodino, and if this or that arrangement had depended on his will, then obviously a cold affecting the exercise of his will might have saved Russia—and consequently, the valet who forgot to bring Napoleon his waterproof boots on the twenty-fourth would have been the savior of Russia. Along that line of reasoning, such a conclusion is indisputable, as indisputable as the conclusion Voltaire jokingly drew (not knowing what he was joking about) when he said that the Massacre of Saint Bartholomew was caused by Charles IX's upset stomach. But to people who do not accept that Russia was formed by the will of one man, Peter I, or that the French Empire was created and the war with Russia begun by the will of one man, Napoleon, that argument seems not merely untrue and irrational but contrary to all human reality. To the question of what causes historic events, a different answer presents itself: the course of human events is predetermined from above—it depends on the combined wills of all who take part in those events, and a Napoleon's influence on their course is purely superficial and illusory.

Strange as it may seem at first glance to suppose that the Massacre of Saint Bartholomew was not caused by Charles IX's will, though he gave the order and thought it was done because of his order; and strange as it may seem to suppose that the slaughter of eighty thousand men at Borodino was not due to Napoleon's will, though he commanded the battle's commencement and conduct and thought it happened because he ordered it; strange as these assumptions appear, human dignity—which tells me that each of us is, if not more, at least not less of a man than the great Napoleon—demands that we accept this answer, and historical investigation abundantly confirms it.
At the battle of Borodino, Napoleon shot at no one and killed no one. That was all done by the soldiers. Therefore it was not he who killed people.

The French soldiers went to kill and be killed at Borodino not because of Napoleon's orders but by their own volition. The whole army—French, Italian, German, Polish, and Dutch—hungry, ragged, and weary of the campaign, felt at the sight of an army blocking their road to Moscow that the wine was drawn and must be drunk. Had Napoleon then forbidden them to fight the Russians, they would have killed him and gone on to fight the Russians, because it was inevitable.

When they heard Napoleon's proclamation offering them, as compensation for mutilation and death, the words of posterity about their having been in the battle before Moscow, they cried "Long live the Emperor!"—just as they had cried "Long live the Emperor!" at the sight of the portrait of the boy poking the globe with a toy stick, and just as they would have cried "Long live the Emperor!" at any nonsense that might be told them. There was nothing left for them to do but cry "Long live the Emperor!" and go fight, in order to win food and rest as conquerors in Moscow. So it was not because of Napoleon's orders that they killed their fellow men.

And it was not Napoleon who directed the course of the battle, for none of his orders were carried out and during the battle he did not know what was happening in front of him. So the way these people slaughtered one another was not decided by Napoleon's will but happened independently of him, according to the combined will of the hundreds of thousands of people who took part in the common action. It only seemed to Napoleon that it all occurred by his will. And so the question whether he had or hadn't a cold has no more historical importance than the cold of the lowliest transport soldier.

Moreover, the claim by various writers that his cold was the reason his battle plans were not as skillful as on previous occasions and his orders during the battle were not as good as before is quite groundless—which again shows that Napoleon's cold on the twenty-sixth of August was insignificant.

The battle plans cited above are not at all worse but are actually better than previous plans by which he had won victories. His orders during the battle were also no worse than before—they were much the same as always. These plans and orders only seem inferior because the battle of Borodino was the first Napoleon did not win. The most profound and excellent plans and orders seem very bad, and every armchair strategist criticizes them with an air of importance, when they relate to a battle that was lost; and the very worst plans and orders seem brilliant, and serious people fill entire volumes proving their merits, when they relate to a battle that was won.
The battle plan drawn up by Weyrother for the battle of Austerlitz was a model of perfection—yet it too was criticized, precisely for its perfection, for its excessive detail.

Napoleon at the battle of Borodino fulfilled his role as the figurehead of authority as well as—and even better than—at other battles. He did nothing harmful to the battle's progress; he deferred to the most reasonable opinions; he caused no confusion, did not contradict himself, did not panic or run from the battlefield, but with his great tact and military experience calmly and with dignity played his part of appearing to command.
